claim: Resolution thresholds were correlated with the individual retina's sampling capacity.
source: We find that resolution thresholds were correlated with the individual retina's sampling capacity
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing correlation between individual cone density and visual acuity thresholds (Figure 2d), with r²=0.45 (p=0.005) for dominant eyes and r²=0.28 (p=0.036) for non-dominant eyes.

claim: Resolution thresholds exceeded what static sampling limits would predict by 18%, on average.
source: exceeded what static sampling limits would predict by 18%, on average
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly, and Figure 2c-d shows visual acuity thresholds exceeding the Nyquist limit (20% and 16% for dominant and non-dominant eyes at 788 nm).

claim: The length and direction of fixational drift motion played a key role in achieving sub-cone diameter resolution.
source: The length and direction of fixational drift motion, previously thought to be primarily random, played a key role in achieving this sub-cone diameter resolution.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing correlation between drift length and visual acuity (Figure 3g), and demonstrates directional tuning of drift towards higher cone density areas (Figure 4d-e).

claim: Fixational drift motion was previously thought to be primarily random.
source: The length and direction of fixational drift motion, previously thought to be primarily random
evidence: This reflects established scientific understanding cited in the introduction, referencing historical views of drift as random jitter (Cornsweet, 1956; Ditchburn and Ginsborg, 1953).

claim: The oculomotor system finely adjusts drift behavior towards retinal areas with higher cone densities within only a few hundred milliseconds to enhance retinal sampling.
source: The oculomotor system finely adjusts drift behavior towards retinal areas with higher cone densities within only a few hundred milliseconds to enhance retinal sampling.
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 2 shows temporal progression of drift directionality, with tuning ratio increasing from 1.5 at 33 ms to 3.0 at 462 ms. Figure 4d shows 49% of drift episodes moved stimulus towards CDC.

claim: Visual acuity measurement has great importance for many real-life scenarios and is the primary diagnostic tool to determine visual function in clinical and optometric settings.
source: the precise measurement of visual acuity, our ability to resolve fine spatial detail by eye, has great importance for many real-life scenarios and is up to this day the primary diagnostic tool to determine visual function in a clinical and optometric setting
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction without specific citation, reflecting common clinical practice.

claim: The widely-believed assumption that the packing density and arrangement of retinal photoreceptors at the foveal center set the limit to visual acuity has never been experimentally confirmed.
source: Quite surprisingly, the widely-believed assumption that the packing density and arrangement of retinal photoreceptors at the foveal center set the limit to this ability has never been experimentally confirmed.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature, motivating the current study. The manuscript later provides the first direct experimental confirmation.

claim: Fovealization optimizes the human eye for high-acuity daytime vision.
source: Fovealization, the morphological and functional specialization of the cellular architecture of the light-sensitive retina optimizes the human eye for high-acuity daytime vision (Caves et al., 2018; Tuten and Harmening, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Caves et al., 2018 and Tuten and Harmening, 2021.

claim: Within the foveola, postreceptoral neurons are displaced centrifugally.
source: Within the central one-degree diameter of the fovea, termed foveola, postreceptoral neurons are displaced centrifugally and the area is free of potentially shadowing blood vessels and glia cells (Hendrickson and Yuodelis, 1984; Syrbe et al., 2018).
evidence: This anatomical fact is supported by citations to Hendrickson and Yuodelis, 1984 and Syrbe et al., 2018.

claim: The foveola is free of potentially shadowing blood vessels and glia cells.
source: Within the central one-degree diameter of the fovea, termed foveola, postreceptoral neurons are displaced centrifugally and the area is free of potentially shadowing blood vessels and glia cells (Hendrickson and Yuodelis, 1984; Syrbe et al., 2018).
evidence: This anatomical fact is supported by citations to Hendrickson and Yuodelis, 1984 and Syrbe et al., 2018.

claim: Foveolar cone photoreceptor outer segments are maximally thinned and densely packed for peak spatial sampling.
source: The outer segments of foveolar cone photoreceptors are maximally thinned and densely packed for peak spatial sampling (Hirsch and Curcio, 1989; Rossi and Roorda, 2010; Williams and Coletta, 1987)
evidence: This anatomical characteristic is supported by citations to Hirsch and Curcio, 1989; Rossi and Roorda, 2010; and Williams and Coletta, 1987.

claim: Foveolar cones are the most difficult photoreceptors to study ex vivo.
source: which at the same time makes these cells the most difficult to study ex vivo (Curcio et al., 1987) as well as in vivo (Rossi et al., 2011)
evidence: This difficulty is supported by citation to Curcio et al., 1987 for ex vivo studies.

claim: Foveolar cones are the most difficult photoreceptors to study in vivo.
source: which at the same time makes these cells the most difficult to study ex vivo (Curcio et al., 1987) as well as in vivo (Rossi et al., 2011)
evidence: This difficulty is supported by citation to Rossi et al., 2011 for in vivo studies.

claim: Each foveolar cone synapses to one ON- and one OFF-midget bipolar cell, which in turn synapse exclusively upon single ON- and OFF-midget ganglion cells.
source: Each foveolar cone synapses to one ON- and one OFF-midget bipolar cell, which in turn synapse exclusively upon single ON- and OFF-midget ganglion cells, a circuit that is adult-like before birth (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This neural circuit architecture is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: The foveolar cone-to-ganglion cell circuit is adult-like before birth.
source: Each foveolar cone synapses to one ON- and one OFF-midget bipolar cell, which in turn synapse exclusively upon single ON- and OFF-midget ganglion cells, a circuit that is adult-like before birth (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This developmental fact is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: The foveolar cone-to-ganglion cell circuit establishes an undisturbed private line from individual foveal receptors to central processing stages.
source: This establishes an undisturbed private line from individual foveal receptors to central processing stages.
evidence: This is inferred from the described one-to-one connectivity pattern between cones and ganglion cells via bipolar cells.

claim: The hypothesis that cone spacing imposes the fundamental limit for visual resolution has been put forward based on indirect comparisons between histological and psychophysical data.
source: Based on indirect comparisons between histological and psychophysical data, the hypothesis that cone spacing imposes the fundamental limit for visual resolution has been put forward (Curcio et al., 1990; Rossi and Roorda, 2010).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citations to Curcio et al., 1990 and Rossi and Roorda, 2010.

claim: Cone spacing, especially in the central fovea, is highly variable between individuals.
source: It is well established that cone spacing, especially in the central fovea, is highly variable between individuals (Cava et al., 2020; Curcio et al., 1990; Reiniger et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2019)
evidence: This variability is supported by citations to Cava et al., 2020; Curcio et al., 1990; Reiniger et al., 2021; and Wang et al., 2019.

claim: Under natural viewing conditions, both visual resolution and experimental access to foveal photoreceptors are blurred by the imperfect optics of the human eye.
source: One of the main reasons why the hypothesis lacks direct experimental proof is that because, under natural viewing conditions, both visual resolution and experimental access to foveal photoreceptors are blurred by the imperfect optics of the human eye (Campbell and Green, 1965; Marcos et al., 2008).
evidence: This optical limitation is supported by citations to Campbell and Green, 1965 and Marcos et al., 2008.

claim: Performance thresholds for different visual tasks can be substantially lower than the sampling grain of photoreceptors, a phenomenon termed hyperacuity.
source: While acuity is assumed to be mainly limited by the resolving capacity of the eye's optics and retinal mosaic, it is well established that, for different visual tasks, performance thresholds can be substantially lower than the sampling grain of photoreceptors. This phenomenon has been termed hyperacuity (Westheimer, 1975)
evidence: This phenomenon is supported by citation to Westheimer, 1975.

claim: Hyperacuity depends on the neural visual system's ability to extract subtle differences within the spatial patterns of the optical image on the retina.
source: This phenomenon has been termed hyperacuity (Westheimer, 1975) and depends on the neural visual system's ability to extract subtle differences within the spatial patterns of the optical image on the retina (Westheimer, 2012).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citation to Westheimer, 2012.

claim: The visual system incorporates mechanisms to detect relative spatial offsets an order of magnitude smaller than the spatial granularity of the retina.
source: Thus, the visual system already incorporates mechanisms to detect relative spatial offsets an order of magnitude smaller than the spatial granularity of the retina.
evidence: This is inferred from the hyperacuity phenomenon described in the previous sentences.

claim: The visual system depends on temporal transients arising in the receptor's cellular signals.
source: Unlike a camera, the visual system depends on temporal transients arising in the receptor's cellular signals.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent citation about neuronal responses to temporal changes.

claim: Neurons in the retina, thalamus, and later stages of the visual pathways respond strongly to temporal changes.
source: Neurons in the retina, thalamus, and later stages of the visual pathways respond strongly to temporal changes (Kaplan and Benardete, 2001; Nagano, 1980).
evidence: This neuronal property is supported by citations to Kaplan and Benardete, 2001 and Nagano, 1980.

claim: Quick and precise eye movements bring retinal images of objects of interest to land in the foveola.
source: Thus, the fovealized retinal architecture in humans is accompanied by a dynamic sampling behavior that, by quick and precise movements of the eye, brings retinal images of objects of interest to land in the foveola (Ko et al., 2010).
evidence: This oculomotor behavior is supported by citation to Ko et al., 2010.

claim: During steady fixation, incessant fixational eye movements slide tens to hundreds of foveolar photoreceptors across the retinal image.
source: Even during steady fixation, for example of a distant face or a single letter of this text, incessant fixational eye movements slide tens to hundreds of foveolar photoreceptors across the retinal image, thereby introducing temporal modulations that translate spatial activation patterns into the temporal domain (Kuang et al., 2012).
evidence: This effect of fixational eye movements is supported by citation to Kuang et al., 2012.

claim: Fixational eye movements introduce temporal modulations that translate spatial activation patterns into the temporal domain.
source: Even during steady fixation, for example of a distant face or a single letter of this text, incessant fixational eye movements slide tens to hundreds of foveolar photoreceptors across the retinal image, thereby introducing temporal modulations that translate spatial activation patterns into the temporal domain (Kuang et al., 2012).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citation to Kuang et al., 2012.

claim: Microsaccades are small and rapid gaze shifts that relocate the gaze within the foveola during periods of fixation.
source: Small and rapid gaze shifts known as microsaccades relocate the gaze within the foveola during periods of fixation (Ko et al., 2010)
evidence: This characterization of microsaccades is supported by citation to Ko et al., 2010.

claim: Between microsaccades, the eyes perform a more continuous, seemingly random motion termed fixational drift.
source: and between microsaccades, the eyes perform a more continuous, seemingly random motion termed fixational drift (Intoy and Rucci, 2020; Krauskopf et al., 1960).
evidence: This characterization of drift is supported by citations to Intoy and Rucci, 2020 and Krauskopf et al., 1960.

claim: Computational work suggested that fixational eye motion would introduce noise and thus impair visual acuity.
source: Computational work suggested that fixational eye motion would introduce noise and thus impair visual acuity (Burak et al., 2010; Pitkow et al., 2007).
evidence: This computational prediction is supported by citations to Burak et al., 2010 and Pitkow et al., 2007.

claim: Recent studies on human psychophysics demonstrated fixational eye motion to be beneficial for fine spatial vision.
source: Contrarily, recent studies on human psychophysics demonstrated fixational eye motion to be beneficial for fine spatial vision (Intoy and Rucci, 2020; Rolfs, 2009; Rucci et al., 2007).
evidence: This beneficial effect is supported by citations to Intoy and Rucci, 2020; Rolfs, 2009; and Rucci et al., 2007.

claim: Drift motion has been increasingly argued to not just be randomly refreshing neural activity, but rather structuring it.
source: Especially drift motion has been increasingly argued to not just be randomly refreshing neural activity, but rather structuring it (Clark et al., 2022; Hafed et al., 2021; Intoy and Rucci, 2020) and being under central control (Herrmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This view of drift is supported by citations to Clark et al., 2022; Hafed et al., 2021; and Intoy and Rucci, 2020.

claim: Drift motion is under central control.
source: Especially drift motion has been increasingly argued to not just be randomly refreshing neural activity, but rather structuring it (Clark et al., 2022; Hafed et al., 2021; Intoy and Rucci, 2020) and being under central control (Herrmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This control mechanism is supported by citation to Herrmann et al., 2017.

claim: Luminance modulation in individual cones scales with drift length.
source: For instance, luminance modulation in individual cones will scale with drift length.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the relationship between eye movement and photoreceptor stimulation.

claim: Larger luminance variations on single receptors yield more neuronal activity within the range of temporal frequencies parvocellular ganglion cells are sensitive to.
source: Larger luminance variations on single receptors also yields more neuronal activity within the range of temporal frequencies parvocellular ganglion cells are sensitive to.
evidence: This is inferred from knowledge of parvocellular ganglion cell properties and their response to temporal modulation.

claim: Selective spatial frequencies can be amplified by varying drift lengths.
source: Selective spatial frequencies can thus be amplified by varying drift lengths (Intoy and Rucci, 2020).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citation to Intoy and Rucci, 2020.

claim: The neuronal mechanisms that generate fixational drift are still not fully understood.
source: While the neuronal mechanisms that generate fixational drift are still not fully understood (Ben-Shushan et al., 2022)
evidence: This gap in understanding is supported by citation to Ben-Shushan et al., 2022.

claim: Drift was shown to improve visual performance in resolution tasks.
source: Drift was shown to improve visual performance in resolution tasks (Intoy and Rucci, 2020; Ratnam et al., 2017; Rucci et al., 2007).
evidence: This improvement is supported by citations to Intoy and Rucci, 2020; Ratnam et al., 2017; and Rucci et al., 2007.

claim: Considerable differences in ocular drift between individuals exist.
source: Indeed, considerable differences in ocular drift between individuals exist (Cherici et al., 2012; Clark et al., 2022)
evidence: This variability is supported by citations to Cherici et al., 2012 and Clark et al., 2022.

claim: Subjects exhibiting less drift were shown to have better acuity.
source: and subjects exhibiting less drift were shown to have better acuity (Clark et al., 2022).
evidence: This relationship is supported by citation to Clark et al., 2022.

claim: Participants reached visual acuity thresholds between 20.6 and 28.5 arcsec (mean ± SD: 24.1±2.4 arcsec), which compares to 20/8 vision (logMAR = –0.4).
source: In this near diffraction-limited testing condition, participants reached visual acuity thresholds between 20.6 and 28.5 arcsec (mean ± SD: 24.1±2.4 arcsec), which compares to 20/8 vision (logMAR = –0.4).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from the psychophysical testing.

claim: All participants reached thresholds better than 20/10 vision (logMAR = –0.3).
source: All participants reached thresholds better than 20/10 vision (logMAR = –0.3), the last line of a typical clinical Snellen chart or projectors of acuity optotypes that are used in clinical as well as optometric daily routine.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from the psychophysical testing.

claim: Cone densities at the cone density centroid ranged between 10,692 and 16,997 cones/deg2, with an average density of 13,640 cones/deg2.
source: Cone densities at the cone density centroid (CDC) ranged between 10,692 and 16,997 cones/deg2, with an average density of 13,640 cones/deg2 (Average peak cone density, PCD: 13,944 cones/deg2, range: 10,823–17,309 cones/deg2), comparable to previous reports (Cava et al., 2020; Putnam et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2019; Wells-Gray et al., 2016; Wilk et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is directly measured anatomical data from the cone mosaic imaging, compared to previous reports.

claim: Average peak cone density was 13,944 cones/deg2, with a range of 10,823–17,309 cones/deg2.
source: Cone densities at the cone density centroid (CDC) ranged between 10,692 and 16,997 cones/deg2, with an average density of 13,640 cones/deg2 (Average peak cone density, PCD: 13,944 cones/deg2, range: 10,823–17,309 cones/deg2), comparable to previous reports (Cava et al., 2020; Putnam et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2019; Wells-Gray et al., 2016; Wilk et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is directly measured anatomical data from the cone mosaic imaging.

claim: The median sampling cone density ranged between 10,297 and 16,104 cones/deg2 (mean: 13,149 cones/deg2).
source: The median sampling cone density ranged between 10,297 and 16,104 cones/deg2 (mean: 13,149 cones/deg2).
evidence: This is computed from the experimental data based on which cones sampled the stimulus.

claim: Visual acuity thresholds exceeded the Nyquist limit predicted by the spacing between rows of cones by 20% and 16% in dominant and non-dominant eyes, respectively, when tested with 788 nm light.
source: On average, visual acuity thresholds exceeded this theoretical prediction by 20% and 16% in dominant and non-dominant eyes, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental visual acuity data compared to the theoretical Nyquist limit based on cone spacing.

claim: When tested with 840 nm light, visual acuity thresholds were on average 7% below and 2% above the Nyquist limit for dominant and non-dominant eyes, respectively.
source: Visual acuity thresholds were on average 7% below and 2% above the Nyquist limit for dominant and non-dominant eyes, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental visual acuity data at 840 nm compared to the theoretical Nyquist limit.

claim: Diffraction-limited visual acuity thresholds were strongly correlated to the foveolar sampling density in dominant as well as fellow eyes.
source: We found the diffraction-limited visual acuity thresholds to be strongly correlated to the foveolar sampling density in dominant as well as fellow eyes (Figure 2d).
evidence: Figure 2d shows the correlation with r²=0.45 (p=0.005) for dominant eyes and r²=0.28 (p=0.036) for non-dominant eyes.

claim: Up to 45% of the variance in inter-subject visual acuity can be explained by the individual cone sampling densities.
source: The degree of correlation slightly differed for dominant (r2=0.45, p=0.005) and non-dominant eyes (r2=0.28, p=0.036), suggesting that up to 45% of the variance in inter-subject visual acuity can be explained by the individual cone sampling densities.
evidence: This is inferred from the r² value of the correlation between cone density and visual acuity.

claim: Participants reached significantly lower thresholds with their dominant eyes (average: 1.5 arcsec, SD ±1.1; paired t-test, p<0.001).
source: Overall, participants reached significantly lower thresholds with their dominant eyes (average: 1.5 arcsec, SD ±1.1; paired t-test, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of measured visual acuity data between dominant and non-dominant eyes.

claim: Visual acuity thresholds were strongly correlated between dominant and non-dominant eyes (r2=0.80, p<0.001).
source: Nevertheless, visual acuity thresholds were strongly correlated between dominant and non-dominant eyes (r2=0.80, p<0.001, Figure 2e).
evidence: Figure 2e shows this strong correlation between fellow eyes.

claim: Sampling densities had a very strong correlation between fellow eyes (r2=0.85, p<0.001).
source: Sampling densities had a very strong correlation between fellow eyes (r2=0.85, p<0.001, Figure 2e)
evidence: Figure 2e shows this strong correlation between fellow eyes.

claim: Sampling densities did not differ between right and left eyes (p=0.38).
source: but did not differ between right and left eyes (p=0.38) nor when grouping them according to ocular dominance (p=0.88).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of cone density data between eyes.

claim: Sampling densities did not differ when grouping eyes according to ocular dominance (p=0.88).
source: but did not differ between right and left eyes (p=0.38) nor when grouping them according to ocular dominance (p=0.88).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of cone density data grouped by dominance.

claim: Dominant eyes had a median of 78 cones/deg2 higher densities compared to their fellow eyes.
source: Dominant eyes had a median of 78 cones/deg2 higher densities compared to their fellow eyes.
evidence: This is calculated from the cone density measurements.

claim: To account for the 1.5 arcsec difference in acuity thresholds between dominant and non-dominant eyes, a density difference of about 1500 cones/deg2 would have been needed.
source: To account for the 1.5 arcsec difference in acuity thresholds, a much higher density difference of about 1500 cones/deg2 would have been needed.
evidence: This is calculated based on the relationship between cone density and acuity thresholds.

claim: The spatial arrangement of foveal cones can only partially predict resolution acuity.
source: Based on these results, we conclude that the spatial arrangement of foveal cones can only partially predict resolution acuity.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the finding that cone density explains only up to 45% of acuity variance and cannot fully account for differences between dominant and non-dominant eyes.

claim: Participants kept coming back to the same few hundreds of cone photoreceptors during the visual acuity task.
source: In our experiments, we revealed that participants kept coming back to the same few hundreds of cone photoreceptors (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 show the retinal locations sampled across trials.

claim: Participants tend to suppress their microsaccades during fine-scale discrimination tasks.
source: During the short stimulus duration, however, microsaccades rarely occurred, as participants tend to suppress their microsaccades, likely because they can be detrimental to fine-scale discrimination (Bowers et al., 2021; Intoy et al., 2021).
evidence: This suppression is supported by citations to Bowers et al., 2021 and Intoy et al., 2021, and observed in the experimental data.

claim: Drift lengths ranged between 2.5 and 17.2 arcmin, with a median length of 6.5 arcmin.
source: Across all participants and experimental trials, drift lengths ranged between 2.5 and 17.2 arcmin, with a median length of 6.5 arcmin (which corresponds to a velocity of 5–34.5 arcmin/s, median: 13 arcmin/s, Figure 3c).
evidence: This is directly measured from the eye tracking data during stimulus presentation.

claim: Drift velocities ranged from 5 to 34.5 arcmin/s, with a median of 13 arcmin/s.
source: Across all participants and experimental trials, drift lengths ranged between 2.5 and 17.2 arcmin, with a median length of 6.5 arcmin (which corresponds to a velocity of 5–34.5 arcmin/s, median: 13 arcmin/s, Figure 3c).
evidence: This is calculated from the drift length measurements over the 500 ms stimulus duration.

claim: The drift lengths observed are slightly smaller than in previous non-AO studies, which is attributable to the viewing situation.
source: The drift lengths are slightly smaller than in previous non-AO studies, which is attributable to the viewing situation. The participants were looking at a very small imaging field within a completely dark periphery without distracting structures or stimuli.
evidence: This comparison is made to previous studies and explained by the experimental conditions.

claim: The smallest drift movement performed was similar among eyes (range: 2.5–5.4 arcmin).
source: The smallest drift movement performed was similar among eyes (range: 2.5–5.4 arcmin)
evidence: This is calculated from the minimum drift lengths across all eyes.

claim: The largest individual drifts differed more than three times as much (range: 7.7–17.2 arcmin).
source: whereas the largest individual drifts differed more than three times as much (range: 7.7–17.2 arcmin).
evidence: This is calculated from the maximum drift lengths across all eyes.

claim: There was a strong correlation between median drift length and drift range (dominant eyes: r2=0.55, p=0.002, non-dominant eyes: r2=0.34, p=0.02).
source: Therefore, the individual drift span was rather driven by the larger drift lengths of an eye and there was a strong correlation between median drift length and drift range (dominant eyes: r2=0.55, p=0.002, non-dominant eyes: r2=0.34, p=0.02, Figure 3d).
evidence: Figure 3d shows this correlation between median drift length and drift range.

claim: Drift lengths in fellow eyes had a very strong correlation (r2=0.86, p<0.001).
source: Between fellow eyes, which were measured consecutively, drift lengths had a very strong correlation (r2=0.86, p<0.001, Figure 3e)
evidence: Figure 3e shows this strong correlation between fellow eyes.

claim: There was no significant difference in drift length between dominant and non-dominant eyes (paired t-test, p=0.2).
source: with no significant difference between eyes (paired t-test, p=0.2).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of drift length data between eyes.

claim: The median drift lengths of all eyes varied between 4.8 and 8.5 arcmin (mean ± SD: 6.6±1.1 arcmin).
source: The median drift lengths of all eyes varied between 4.8 and 8.5 arcmin (mean ± SD: 6.6±1.1 arcmin).
evidence: This is calculated from the drift length measurements across all eyes.

claim: Individual visual acuity thresholds were significantly correlated with drift lengths (dominant: r2=0.25, p=0.04; non-dominant: r2=0.29, p=0.03).
source: Individual visual acuity thresholds were significantly correlated with drift lengths (dominant: r2=0.25, p=0.04; non-dominant: r2=0.29, p=0.03, Figure 3g)
evidence: Figure 3g shows this correlation with a trend towards better acuity for smaller drift.

claim: There is a trend towards better visual acuity for small ocular drift motion.
source: Individual visual acuity thresholds were significantly correlated with drift lengths (dominant: r2=0.25, p=0.04; non-dominant: r2=0.29, p=0.03, Figure 3g), with a trend towards better visual acuity for small ocular drift motion.
evidence: This trend is observed in Figure 3g showing the correlation between drift length and acuity.

claim: There was no significant correlation between cone densities and drift length (dominant: r2=0.07, p=0.3; non-dominant: r2=0.06, p=0.4).
source: There was no significant correlation between cone densities and drift length (Figure 3f, dominant: r2=0.07, p=0.3; non-dominant: r2=0.06, p=0.4).
evidence: Figure 3f shows the lack of correlation between these variables.

claim: 49% of all drift episodes moved the stimulus towards the CDC ± 45°.
source: We observed a strong trend of drift directionality; 49% of all drift episodes moved the stimulus towards the CDC ± 45° (Figure 4d).
evidence: Figure 4d shows the distribution of drift directions relative to CDC.

claim: Among eyes, the individual fractions of drift towards CDC ranged between 16 and 80% of trials.
source: Among eyes, the individual fractions ranged between 16 and 80% of trials.
evidence: This range is calculated from the individual eye data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only two eyes drifted towards the CDC less frequently than given by chance.
source: Only two eyes drifted towards the CDC less frequently than given by chance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1 shows the individual eye drift directionality data.

claim: Directionality tuning ratios ranged between 0.6 and 11.8 with a median value of 3.
source: The directionality tuning ratios ranged between 0.6 and 11.8 with a median value of 3.
evidence: This is calculated from the drift directionality data across all eyes.

claim: Directionality tuning ratios had a significant effect on how much the resolution threshold exceeded the Nyquist limit (dominant eyes: r2=0.45, p=0.01; non-dominant eyes: r2=0.27, p=0.04).
source: Directionality tuning ratios had a significant effect on how much the resolution threshold exceeded the Nyquist limit. Participants with highly tuned drift reached larger differences between the Nyquist limit and their visual acuity threshold (dominant eyes: r2=0.45, p=0.01; non-dominant eyes: r2=0.27, p=0.04, Figure 4e).
evidence: Figure 4e shows this correlation between tuning ratio and threshold difference from Nyquist limit.

claim: The retinae moved the stimulus towards the PRL or PCD location in 42% or 35% of all trials, respectively.
source: When relating the drift trajectories to the preferred retinal locus of fixation (PRL) or the location of peak cone density (PCD), we found a weaker approximation towards both. The retinae moved the stimulus towards the PRL or PCD location in 42% or 35% of all trials, respectively (Figure 4f).
evidence: Figure 4f shows the distribution of drift directions relative to PRL and PCD.

claim: The observed directionality was strongest towards the CDC compared to PRL or PCD.
source: Therefore, the observed directionality was strongest towards the CDC.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing the percentages of drift towards CDC (49%), PRL (42%), and PCD (35%).

claim: There was a significant reduction of the isoline contour area (ISOA) size between stimulus onset and offset (p=0.02).
source: Across participants, this also resulted in a significant reduction of the isoline contour area (ISOA) size between stimulus onset and offset (p=0.02, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 4b and Video 3).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of ISOA sizes, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 4b and Video 3.

claim: The median ISOA for stimulus onset locations was 92.5 arcmin2 which was reduced to 68.2 arcmin2 for stimulus offset locations.
source: The median ISOA for stimulus onset locations was 92.5 arcmin2 which was reduced to 68.2 arcmin2 for stimulus offset locations.
evidence: This is calculated from the spatial distribution of stimulus landing positions.

claim: The median distance convergence towards CDC, PRL, and PCD was about 12%, 7%, and 3%, respectively.
source: When we looked at how much the individual drift trajectory decreased the distance from either location, the median distance convergence (onset/offset distance) towards CDC, PRL, and PCD was about 12%, 7%, and 3%, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from the drift trajectory data relative to each landmark.

claim: No participant had an average convergence of more than 30% towards PRL or PCD.
source: While no participant had an average convergence of more than 30% towards PRL or PCD, the maximum convergence ratio towards CDC was about 50%.
evidence: This is calculated from the convergence data across all participants.

claim: The maximum convergence ratio towards CDC was about 50%.
source: While no participant had an average convergence of more than 30% towards PRL or PCD, the maximum convergence ratio towards CDC was about 50%.
evidence: This is calculated from the convergence data across all participants.

claim: Eyes exhibited significantly larger drift lengths when the stimulus onset location was further away from the CDC (ρ2=0.06, p<0.001).
source: Although the individual drift lengths could vary substantially from trial to trial, we found that, across all participants and experimental trials, eyes exhibited significantly larger drift lengths when the stimulus onset location was further away from the CDC (ρ2=0.06, p<0.001, Figure 4g).
evidence: Figure 4g shows this correlation between onset distance from CDC and drift length.

claim: The onset distance was not correlated with drift directionality.
source: The onset distance was not correlated with drift directionality (Figure 4g).
evidence: Figure 4g shows drift direction (color-coded) is not systematically related to onset distance.

claim: The average sampling cone density increased between stimulus onset and offset for most of the participants.
source: Across all trials, the average sampling cone density increased between stimulus onset and offset for most of the participants.
evidence: This is calculated from the cone density at different retinal locations during each trial.

claim: The sampling gain was significantly correlated with the potential retinal sampling gain of individuals in dominant (r2=0.35, p=0.02) as well as non-dominant eyes (r2=0.50, p=0.002).
source: The sampling gain was significantly correlated with the potential retinal sampling gain of individuals in dominant (r2=0.35, p=0.02) as well as non-dominant eyes (r2=0.50, p=0.002, Figure 4h).
evidence: Figure 4h shows this correlation between achieved and potential sampling gain.

claim: Observers exploited on average 30% of their potential sampling gain in both fellow eyes.
source: Observers exploited on average 30% of their potential sampling gain in both fellow eyes.
evidence: This is calculated from the sampling gain data shown in Figure 4h.

claim: By shifting the stimulus towards the CDC in 50% of cases, the potential sampling gain within individual eyes was exploited by 30%, on average, which goes along with a cone density increase of 3% or 285 cones/deg2.
source: By shifting the stimulus towards the CDC in 50% of cases, the potential sampling gain within individual eyes was exploited by 30%, on average, which goes along with a cone density increase of 3% or 285 cones/deg2.
evidence: This is calculated from the sampling gain and cone density data.

claim: The best corrected visual acuity of young and healthy adults is usually between 20/20 and 20/12.5 (60 and 37.5 arcsec).
source: Measured in daily routine or clinical studies, the best corrected visual acuity of young and healthy adults is usually between 20/20 and 20/12.5 (60 and 37.5 arcsec) (Reiniger et al., 2019; Rossi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Reiniger et al., 2019 and Rossi et al., 2007.

claim: Higher order aberrations inherently blur the retinal image, depending on their magnitude.
source: Even if lower order aberrations are corrected by e.g., glasses or contact lenses, higher order aberrations inherently blur the retinal image, depending on their magnitude (Reiniger et al., 2019).
evidence: This optical effect is supported by citation to Reiniger et al., 2019.

claim: Adaptive optics induce a close-to-diffraction limited optical correction, where the optical improvement is significantly correlated with an increase in visual acuity thresholds.
source: Adaptive optics induce a close-to-diffraction limited optical correction, where the optical improvement is significantly correlated with an increase in visual acuity thresholds (Marcos et al., 2008).
evidence: This effect of adaptive optics is supported by citation to Marcos et al., 2008.

claim: By correcting aberrations with AOSLO, Snellen-E thresholds were measured that were up to half the size (between 20/10 and 20/6.9; 30–20.6 arcsec) compared to the natural viewing condition.
source: By correcting aberrations with AOSLO, we measured Snellen-E thresholds that were up to half the size (between 20/10 and 20/6.9; 30–20.6 arcsec) compared to the natural viewing condition.
evidence: This is a comparison of the measured data to typical natural viewing acuity.

claim: The measured thresholds are slightly lower than previously presented data, very likely because of the different wavelengths used for experimentation.
source: This is slightly lower than previously presented data (Rossi et al., 2007), very likely because of the different wavelengths used for experimentation (Figure 2c).
evidence: This comparison is made to Rossi et al., 2007, with the wavelength difference shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Observers are, to some degree, adapted to their own aberrations.
source: Even though observers are, to some degree, adapted to their own aberrations (Artal et al., 2004)
evidence: This adaptation is supported by citation to Artal et al., 2004.

claim: The best subjective image quality is seen when on average 88% of the aberrations are corrected.
source: the best subjective image quality is seen when on average 88% of the aberrations are corrected (Chen et al., 2007).
evidence: This finding is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2007.

claim: Under normal viewing conditions, optical aberrations and not cone topography may play the dominant role in limiting the eye's acuity.
source: This may indicate that, under normal viewing conditions, optical aberrations and not cone topography may play the dominant role in limiting the eye's acuity.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that observers prefer partial aberration correction and that acuity improves substantially with AO correction.

claim: In the periphery, midget retinal ganglion cell sampling dominates resolution.
source: While in the periphery, midget retinal ganglion cell sampling dominates resolution, resolution of the foveal center was estimated to be governed by the cone sampling limit (Rossi and Roorda, 2010; Williams, 1985).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, with the foveal comparison supported by citations.

claim: Resolution of the foveal center was estimated to be governed by the cone sampling limit.
source: While in the periphery, midget retinal ganglion cell sampling dominates resolution, resolution of the foveal center was estimated to be governed by the cone sampling limit (Rossi and Roorda, 2010; Williams, 1985).
evidence: This estimate is supported by citations to Rossi and Roorda, 2010 and Williams, 1985.

claim: The individual spatial arrangement of cones was highly correlated to the visual acuity of participants and explains up to 45% of its variance.
source: We found that the individual spatial arrangement of cones was highly correlated to the visual acuity of participants and explains up to 45% of its variance (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Eyes with higher foveolar sampling capacity reached lower thresholds than eyes with less densely packed cone photoreceptors.
source: Eyes with higher foveolar sampling capacity reached lower thresholds than eyes with less densely packed cone photoreceptors.
evidence: This is observed in the correlation between cone density and acuity shown in Figure 2d.

claim: All participants reached resolution thresholds that exceeded the static Nyquist sampling limit when tested with near-infrared, 788 nm light.
source: Moreover, all participants reached resolution thresholds that exceeded the static Nyquist sampling limit when tested with near-infrared, 788 nm light.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2c-d where all 788 nm thresholds are below the Nyquist limit line.

claim: The L- and M-cone photopigment absorbance for 840 nm is about 1.4 log unit lower than for 788 nm.
source: The L- and M-cone photopigment absorbance for 840 nm is about 1.4 log unit lower than for 788 nm (Stockman and Rider, 2023).
evidence: This photopigment property is supported by citation to Stockman and Rider, 2023.

claim: The Airy-Disk size is about 7% larger for 840 nm compared to 788 nm.
source: The decreased cone sensitivity combined with a larger Airy-Disk size of about 7% are likely to be detrimental for the longer, 840 nm, wavelength.
evidence: This is calculated from the wavelength difference and optical principles.

claim: Myopic eyes generally have a higher angular sampling density in and around the foveola, compared to emmetropes.
source: Myopic eyes, despite retinal stretching, generally have a higher angular sampling density in and around the foveola, compared to emmetropes (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This anatomical characteristic is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2019.

claim: If the retinal image is under-sampled, aliasing occurs at the frequency of the receptor mosaic, which may obscure the original image, especially its orientation.
source: If the retinal image is under-sampled, aliasing occurs at the frequency of the receptor mosaic, which may obscure the original image, especially its orientation (compare example snapshots in Figure 1f).
evidence: This is a principle from sampling theory, illustrated in Figure 1f.

claim: Prior knowledge of the stimulus has been shown to theoretically help to de-alias under-sampled signals even in a static condition.
source: While prior knowledge of the stimulus has been shown to theoretically help to de-alias under-sampled signals even in a static condition (Ruderman and Bialek, 1992)
evidence: This theoretical possibility is supported by citation to Ruderman and Bialek, 1992.

claim: Retinal image motion plays a significant role in deciphering orientation at the limits of spatial sampling.
source: we believe that retinal image motion plays a significant role in deciphering orientation at the limits of spatial sampling.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation based on their experimental findings.

claim: Fixational eye movements continuously modulate the luminance flow on individual cones and postreceptoral neuronal activity.
source: Fixational eye movements continuously modulate the luminance flow on individual cones and postreceptoral neuronal activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the effect of eye movements on neural signals.

claim: Drift motion is beneficial for psychophysical measures of visual acuity in the parafovea.
source: More recent work revealed that drift motion is neither random (Rucci and Poletti, 2015) nor detrimental due to the introduction of noise (Burak et al., 2010; Pitkow et al., 2007), but rather a fine-tuned motion, beneficial for psychophysical measures of visual acuity in the parafovea (Ratnam et al., 2017) as well as foveola (Intoy and Rucci, 2020).
evidence: This beneficial effect is supported by citation to Ratnam et al., 2017.

claim: Drift motion is beneficial for psychophysical measures of visual acuity in the foveola.
source: More recent work revealed that drift motion is neither random (Rucci and Poletti, 2015) nor detrimental due to the introduction of noise (Burak et al., 2010; Pitkow et al., 2007), but rather a fine-tuned motion, beneficial for psychophysical measures of visual acuity in the parafovea (Ratnam et al., 2017) as well as foveola (Intoy and Rucci, 2020).
evidence: This beneficial effect is supported by citation to Intoy and Rucci, 2020.

claim: Neurons in the visual system are strongly selective not just for spatial patterns, but also for temporally changing stimuli.
source: As also observed in other sensory organs (Ahissar and Arieli, 2001), neurons in the visual system are strongly selective not just for spatial patterns, but also for temporally changing stimuli (Ahissar and Arieli, 2012)
evidence: This neuronal property is supported by citations to Ahissar and Arieli, 2001 and 2012.

claim: Computational modeling suggests that the visual system may utilize principles comparable to those used in computational imaging for achieving super-resolution via camera motion.
source: a finding that is also supported by computational modeling, suggesting that the visual system may utilize principles comparable to those used in computational imaging for achieving super-resolution via camera motion (Anderson et al., 2020).
evidence: This computational modeling is supported by citation to Anderson et al., 2020.

claim: The indirect suppression of natural fixational eye motion by retinal stabilization techniques impairs visual acuity outside the foveolar center.
source: Contrary, the indirect suppression of natural fixational eye motion by retinal stabilization techniques impairs visual acuity outside the foveolar center (Intoy and Rucci, 2020; Rucci et al., 2007).
evidence: This impairment is supported by citations to Intoy and Rucci, 2020 and Rucci et al., 2007.

claim: For prolonged static stimulus presentations, retinal spiking decays over time.
source: For prolonged static stimulus presentations, retinal spiking decays over time, while drift motion keeps the luminance change active, continuously refreshes the receptive field input, and sustains neuronal activity (Kuang et al., 2012).
evidence: This neural response pattern is supported by citation to Kuang et al., 2012.

claim: Drift motion keeps the luminance change active, continuously refreshes the receptive field input, and sustains neuronal activity.
source: For prolonged static stimulus presentations, retinal spiking decays over time, while drift motion keeps the luminance change active, continuously refreshes the receptive field input, and sustains neuronal activity (Kuang et al., 2012).
evidence: This effect of drift is supported by citation to Kuang et al., 2012.

claim: Acuity improved for smaller fixational drift and decreased in participants who exhibited larger drift motion, on average.
source: Interestingly, acuity improved for smaller fixational drift and decreased in participants who exhibited larger drift motion, on average.
evidence: This is observed in the correlation shown in Figure 3g.

claim: Smaller drifts induce luminance changes with higher spatial frequencies.
source: The fact that less drift is beneficial to reach the lowest possible acuity thresholds reflects the characteristics of spatiotemporal luminance changes introduced by smaller or larger drift motion. Smaller drifts induce luminance changes with higher spatial frequencies
evidence: This is inferred from the relationship between drift length and spatial frequency of stimulation.

claim: Models of retinal ganglion cell activity suggest a higher contrast sensitivity for high spatial frequency motion and less for low spatial frequencies compared to a static retina.
source: and models of retinal ganglion cell activity suggest a higher contrast sensitivity for high spatial frequency motion and less for low spatial frequencies compared to a static retina (Kuang et al., 2012; Rucci and Victor, 2015).
evidence: This modeling result is supported by citations to Kuang et al., 2012 and Rucci and Victor, 2015.

claim: Visual acuity thresholds can be predicted from drift magnitudes measured in a sustained fixation task.
source: This is supported by other recent work which also showed that visual acuity thresholds can even be predicted from drift magnitudes measured in a sustained fixation task (Clark et al., 2022).
evidence: This predictive relationship is supported by citation to Clark et al., 2022.

claim: A previous study in macaque monkeys revealed a systematic directional drift response only a few dozens of milliseconds after various visual transients.
source: A previous study in macaque monkeys revealed a systematic directional drift response only a few dozens of milliseconds after various visual transients (Malevich et al., 2020).
evidence: This finding in macaques is supported by citation to Malevich et al., 2020.

claim: Human observers are capable of adapting their drift direction to enact an oculomotor strategy that takes advantage of the maximum resolution capacity provided within the retina.
source: In our study, we reveal that a certain drift directionality can not only be triggered by particular visual transients, but that human observers are capable of adapting their drift direction to enact an oculomotor strategy that takes advantage of the maximum resolution capacity provided within the retina.
evidence: This is the main finding from the drift directionality analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Participants precisely moved their eyes to have the stimulus slip across the most densely packed cone cells within their foveola.
source: Our participants precisely moved their eyes to have the stimulus slip across the most densely packed cone cells within their foveola.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the directional tuning towards CDC shown in Figure 4d-f.

claim: Drift can be quickly adjusted in a continuous closed-loop control.
source: This confirms that drift can be quickly adjusted in a continuous closed-loop control (Gruber and Ahissar, 2020)
evidence: This control mechanism is supported by citation to Gruber and Ahissar, 2020.

claim: Specific task knowledge influences the dominant orientation of drift, even in the sudden absence of visual information.
source: while, as other recent work suggests, being at the same time able to quickly switch to an open-loop process, as specific task knowledge influences the dominant orientation of drift, even in the sudden absence of visual information (Lin et al., 2023).
evidence: This finding is supported by citation to Lin et al., 2023.

claim: Based on brainstem recordings in rhesus monkeys, the origin of drift can be found mostly upstream of the ocular motoneurons.
source: Recent work suggested, based on brainstem recordings in rhesus monkeys, that the origin can be found mostly upstream of the ocular motoneurons. It can likely be explained as diffusion in the oculomotor integrator which is mainly driven by noise, but additionally affected by mechanisms within the visual motor pathway (e.g. feedback mechanisms) (Ben-Shushan et al., 2022).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citation to Ben-Shushan et al., 2022.

claim: An incorporation of a visual feedback loop to the oculomotor model was shown to modulate the statistics of eye motion, given a time lag of about 100 ms.
source: An incorporation of a visual feedback loop to that model was shown to modulate the statistics of eye motion, given a time lag of about 100 ms (mainly due to synaptic processing delays, of order 60–80ms Malevich et al., 2020).
evidence: This modeling result is supported by citation to Malevich et al., 2020.

claim: The presentation time of 500 ms sufficed for a modulation of the fixational drift motion towards retinal areas of higher cone sampling.
source: This fits our results well. Our presentation time of 500 ms sufficed for a modulation of the fixational drift motion towards retinal areas of higher cone sampling (also see Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the temporal progression of drift directionality shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Some aspects of the statistics of drift motion can be influenced by the visual task.
source: Our data supports the view that some aspects of the statistics of drift motion can be influenced by the visual task (Ben-Shushan et al., 2022; Intoy and Rucci, 2020; Malevich et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2023).
evidence: This view is supported by citations to Ben-Shushan et al., 2022; Intoy and Rucci, 2020; Malevich et al., 2020; and Zhao et al., 2023, as well as the current data.

claim: The superior colliculus seems to play a major role in modulating drift motion in a feedback loop to visual inputs.
source: The superior colliculus seems to play a major role in modulating drift motion in a feedback loop to visual inputs (Hafed et al., 2021).
evidence: This role is supported by citation to Hafed et al., 2021.

claim: The superior colliculus is involved in controlling large eye motions.
source: It's not only involved in controlling large eye motions (Bergeron et al., 2003) and microsaccades (Hafed et al., 2009)
evidence: This role is supported by citation to Bergeron et al., 2003.

claim: The superior colliculus is involved in controlling microsaccades.
source: It's not only involved in controlling large eye motions (Bergeron et al., 2003) and microsaccades (Hafed et al., 2009)
evidence: This role is supported by citation to Hafed et al., 2009.

claim: The superior colliculus reflects neural responses to fixational drift that are likely a result of sensory input.
source: but also reflects neural responses to fixational drift that are likely a result of sensory input (C.-Y. Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This neural response is supported by citation to C.-Y. Chen et al., 2019.

claim: The CDC is displaced from the PRL in a way to be beneficial for natural binocular vision.
source: So, even though the CDC is displaced from the PRL in a way to be beneficial for natural binocular vision (Reiniger et al., 2021)
evidence: This displacement and its benefit is supported by citation to Reiniger et al., 2021.

claim: Constant visual feedback allows to adapt the drift direction and, therefore, also the task-related PRL.
source: constant visual feedback allows to adapt the drift direction and, therefore, also the task-related PRL.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed directional drift and shift in PRL between tasks.

claim: The PRL is very reproducible.
source: Commonly, the term PRL is used for describing the retinal location that is preferably used in fixational tasks. It is still a matter of debate what factors drive the development of this very reproducible (Reiniger et al., 2021) retinal location
evidence: This reproducibility is supported by citation to Reiniger et al., 2021.

claim: Sensitivity to small light spots in the foveola seems to be rather plateau-like and not particularly pronounced at the PRL.
source: Sensitivity to small light spots in the foveola seems to be rather plateau-like and not particularly pronounced at the PRL (Domdei et al., 2021).
evidence: This finding is supported by citation to Domdei et al., 2021.

claim: The PRL slightly differs between different tasks but has a larger interindividual variability.
source: As recently shown, the PRL slightly differs between different tasks but has a larger interindividual variability (Bowers et al., 2021).
evidence: This variability is supported by citation to Bowers et al., 2021.

claim: The PRL is not necessarily the center of the sampling drift motion when measuring visual resolution.
source: The here shown results indicate that also when measuring visual resolution, the PRL is not necessarily the center of the sampling drift motion.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the stronger directionality towards CDC than PRL shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The directional drift motion leads to a shift of the preferred retinal location for a resolution task towards the CDC.
source: The directional drift motion leads to a shift of the preferred retinal location for a resolution task towards the CDC (Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Video 3).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Video 3 show the shift in PRL between fixation and resolution tasks.

claim: 5 out of 8 participants shifted their PRL in a Snellen E task closer to the CDC compared to the PRL for fixating a static disk stimulus in a previous study.
source: However, 5 out of 8 participants also shifted their PRL in a Snellen E task closer to the CDC compared to the PRL for fixating a static disk stimulus (Bowers et al., 2021), the conditions that are best comparable to our study.
evidence: This comparison is made to findings from Bowers et al., 2021.

claim: OCT-derived measures of outer segment length or retinal thickness have been shown to serve for estimates of cone density.
source: For clinical studies of retinal health and in new therapeutical approaches, photoreceptor health and visual acuity can be related to other more standard clinical measures as OCT-derived measures of outer segment length or retinal thickness which have been shown to serve for estimates of cone density (Domdei et al., 2023).
evidence: This relationship is supported by citation to Domdei et al., 2023.

claim: The study included 38 participants who underwent preliminary screening.
source: A total of 38 participants with White ethnicity underwent a preliminary screening where ocular biometry, ophthalmologic status, fixational eye motion, and adaptive optics correction as well as foveolar image quality were tested.
evidence: This is a description of the study population and screening process.

claim: 20 participants with normal ophthalmologic status, resolvable foveolar cones, and ocular anatomy that allowed for a 7 mm pupil aperture were chosen for subsequent examination.
source: From those, 20 participants with normal ophthalmologic status, resolvable foveolar cones, and ocular anatomy that allowed for a 7 mm pupil aperture during experimentation were chosen for subsequent examination.
evidence: This describes the selection criteria and final study population.

claim: The study included 6 male and 14 female observers.
source: All 6 male and 14 female observers (17 adults [age: 18–42], three children [age: 10, 12, and 14]) had no or only mild refractive errors (SE:±2.5 diopters).
evidence: This describes the demographic composition of the study population.

claim: The study included 17 adults (age: 18–42) and three children (age: 10, 12, and 14).
source: All 6 male and 14 female observers (17 adults [age: 18–42], three children [age: 10, 12, and 14]) had no or only mild refractive errors (SE:±2.5 diopters).
evidence: This describes the age distribution of the study population.

claim: All participants had no or only mild refractive errors (SE:±2.5 diopters).
source: All 6 male and 14 female observers (17 adults [age: 18–42], three children [age: 10, 12, and 14]) had no or only mild refractive errors (SE:±2.5 diopters).
evidence: This describes the refractive status of the study population.

claim: The children and 15 adults were naïve participants and two adults were experienced observers.
source: The children and 15 adults were naïve participants and two adults were experienced observers.
evidence: This describes the experience level of participants.

claim: 16 participants were tested with 788 nm light and 12 participants with 840 nm light.
source: The experiments were conducted under two different light conditions (16 participants 788 nm, 12 participants 840 nm).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claim: Eight participants took part in both experimental conditions (788 nm and 840 nm).
source: Eight participants took part in both experimental conditions.
evidence: This describes the overlap in experimental conditions.

claim: The directionality was not pronounced directly after stimulus onset but increased with presentation duration.
source: The directionality was not pronounced directly after stimulus onset but increased with presentation duration (Rayleigh test for circular non-uniformity, p<0.001 for all conditions, see Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 2 shows the temporal progression of directionality with statistical testing.
